q: What is operator overloading in VHDL? Explain with an example.
a: VHDL defines arithmetic only for INTEGER and Boolean ops only for BIT in the Standard package.

Operator overloading defines these functions for other types by writing a function whose name is the operator in double quotes, e.g. function "+"(L: STD_LOGIC_VECTOR; R: STD_LOGIC_VECTOR) return STD_LOGIC_VECTOR
;Normally declared in a package (IEEE std_logic_unsigned) for global visibility.
Example: USE ieee.std_logic_unsigned.all; ports a, b : STD_LOGIC_VECTOR(3 downto 0); sum : STD_LOGIC_VECTOR(4 downto 0); PROCESS(a,b) BEGIN sum <= a + b; END PROCESS;

q: Explain implied and explicit processes, and the rules for sensitivity lists and WAIT statements.
a: Implied processes: concurrent signal assignments, component statements; sensitivity = read side of expression.
Explicit process: PROCESS(sensitivity_list) declarations BEGIN sequential statements END PROCESS; – a concurrent statement made of sequential statements.

A process runs infinitely unless broken by WAIT or a sensitivity list; a sensitivity list implies WAIT at the end; multiple WAITs allowed; never both a sensitivity list and WAIT; synthesis restricts them.
PROCESS(a,b) ... END PROCESS equals PROCESS ... WAIT ON a,b; END PROCESS.

q: Distinguish inertial and transport delay.
a: Signal assignments incur delay, inside or outside processes.
Inertial (default): a pulse shorter than the propagation delay is not transmitted (filtered).
Transport: every pulse is transmitted, however short.

q: Explain the VHDL simulation cycle.
a: Event = a change in value (0→1, X→1).
Cycle has wall-clock time and delta; delta = process execution phase + signal update phase.
Flow: initialize signals → execute all processes (initialization) → advance time → execute sensitive processes → update signals → repeat (delta).
A cycle ends when all processes have executed and signals are updated; signals update at the end of a process.

q: Compare signals and variables in VHDL.

Utility: signals represent circuit interconnect; variables represent local storage.
Scope: signals global (declared outside processes, communicate between processes); variables local (inside a process).
Behaviour: signals updated at end of process (new value not available); variables updated immediately (new value available).

Inversion (VG > Vt): electrons attracted to the surface forming an n-type inversion layer (channel).

Saturation: VDS > VGS − Vt, channel pinches off at the drain; current saturates; the drain depletion field sweeps electrons across, so current continues.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Explain oxidation in IC fabrication.
a: Formation of SiO2 on the wafer surface.
Purposes: protect from contaminants; insulate between conductors; barrier to dopants in diffusion/implantation; grows above and into the silicon.
SiO2 is hard and resists almost all reagents except HF; selective etching opens windows for diffusion.
Wafers in a quartz boat inside a quartz furnace tube at 950–1150 °C with O2 and/or H2O.
Wet: Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2 (fast, lower quality); dry: Si + O2 → SiO2 (slow, higher quality).
Thin oxide (deposited) for gate insulator; field oxide (grown, wet 900–1000 °C or dry 1200 °C) insulates non-active areas.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Explain photolithography and the patterning of materials.
a: Coat the wafer with photoresist.
Shine UV light through a mask to selectively expose the PR.
Dissolve the exposed PR with acid (developer).
Use exposed areas for selective doping or selective removal of the material beneath.
Patterning: add material (poly, metal, oxide via deposition, sputtering, oxidation) → coat PR → selectively remove PR → etch exposed material → remove remaining PR.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Explain diffusion and ion implantation.
a: Diffusion: introduce dopant (arsenic for n, boron for p) via epitaxy or implant; drive in at high temperature; block with oxide or PR; spreads vertically and horizontally.
Ion implantation: ions from a source are mass-selected by a 90° analysing magnet, accelerated (5–200 keV) and scanned in X/Y onto the wafer; 10^-5 Torr, 5 sccm; gases AsH3, PH3, B11F3, etc.
Sequence: grow oxide, photoresist, expose, etch (HF), implant, diffuse (anneal).

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Describe the nMOS fabrication process with sketches.
a: 1 p-type single-crystal Si wafer.
2 Grow thick SiO2 (~1 µm).
3 Spin photoresist.
4 Expose PR to UV through a mask defining diffusion regions and channels.
5 Etch PR and oxide to open a window.
6 Remove PR, grow thin oxide (800–1000 Å), deposit polysilicon (1–2 µm).
7 Pattern poly; remove thin oxide; n+ diffusion (~1 µm) self-aligned to the gate.
8 Grow thick oxide; etch contact cuts to gate, source, drain.
9 Deposit aluminium (~1 µm); pattern interconnects.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)

p-well: n-substrate for pMOS; deep p-well (4–5 µm) for nMOS.

Mask 1 p-well; Mask 2 thinox; Mask 3 polysilicon; Mask 4 p-plus (ANDed with Mask 2) for p-diffusion; Mask 5 negative p-plus for n-diffusion; Mask 6 contact cuts; Mask 7 metal; Mask 8 overglass openings for bonding pads.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Explain the n-well and twin-tub CMOS processes.
a: n-well: p-substrate holds nMOS, n-well holds pMOS; widely accepted, initially as a retrofit to nMOS lines.
Twin-tub: logical extension; start with high-resistivity n-type substrate (with epitaxial layer) and create both n-well and p-well.
Preserves n-transistor performance without compromising p-transistors; easier doping control; relaxed tolerances; particularly important for latch-up.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: What is BiCMOS? State its advantages and features.
a: Bipolar-compatible CMOS, introduced early 1980s, combining bipolar and CMOS logic.
CMOS advantages: low power dissipation, high packing density, high noise margin, high input impedance.
Bipolar advantages: high speed, high output drive, high transconductance gm.
Realised by adding bipolar steps to a baseline CMOS process; BiCMOS gates speed up VLSI.
Dominant for high-speed, low-power, highly functional VLSI; drawback: increased process complexity.

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)
q: Compare characteristics of bipolar and CMOS technologies.
a: Bipolar: higher switching speed; higher current drive per area and gain; better noise and HF performance; improved I/O speed; high power dissipation; lower input impedance; low packing density; low delay sensitivity to load; unidirectional.

CMOS: lower static power; higher noise margins; higher packing density; high yield; high input impedance; scalable threshold; high delay-load sensitivity; low output drive; bidirectional; near-ideal switch; low gain.

Grow P-epitaxy; open two windows; diffuse N-wells (pMOS well and BJT collector).
Open three windows for NMOS, PMOS, NPN BJT; thin oxide + poly patterned as gates.
Moderate p doping → P-base.
Heavy n doping → NMOS S/D, BJT emitter, collector contact.
Heavy p doping → PMOS S/D, base contact.
Thick oxide, contact cuts, metal contacts (S G D, S G D, C B E).

t: Fabrication (nMOS, CMOS, BiCMOS, BJT, R & C)

2 Grow n epitaxial layer.
3 p+ isolation diffusion to isolate devices.
4 p-type base diffusion.
5 n+ emitter diffusion (and collector contact).
6 p+ ohmic base contact.
7 Contact etching.
8 Metal deposition and etching.
9 Passivation and bond pad opening.

Thickness t is fixed by the process, so define Rs = ρ/t (Ω/square).
R = Rs × (L/W); L/W = number of squares.
A square (L = W) has R = Rs regardless of size; e.g. 100 Ω/sq × 5 squares = 500 Ω.

Metal: mΩ/sq, serpentine for 1–10 Ω.
n-well for medium values; n+/p+ diffusions for low values; tolerance 20–50%.

MOS capacitor: gate (metal/poly) one terminal, body grounded; easy to build but capacitance varies with VG due to depletion and inversion.
MIM: two metal plates with insulator; extra process step adds a metal layer close to another; capacitance independent of bias; smaller than MOS capacitors.
Interpoly capacitors are also available in n-well CMOS.

Test, assembly & packaging: wafer test → dicing → die bond → wire bond → encapsulation → test & burn-in.

q: Derive the drain current equations of an nMOS transistor in the linear and saturation regions.
a: Channel charge: gate-oxide-channel is a capacitor, Qch = CV with C = Cg = εoxWL/tox = CoxWL and V = (Vgs − Vds/2) − Vt.
Carrier velocity v = µE with E = Vds/L; transit time t = L/v = L²/(µVds).
Ids = Qch/t = µCox(W/L)(Vgs − Vt − Vds/2)Vds = β(Vgs − Vt − Vds/2)Vds, β = µCoxW/L.
Saturation: for Vds ≥ Vdsat = Vgs − Vt, substitute Vds = Vdsat → Ids = (β/2)(Vgs − Vt)².
Cutoff: Ids = 0 for Vgs < Vt.

q: State the Shockley first-order MOS model and the conditions for each region.

Saturation: Ids = (β/2)(Vgs − Vt)² for Vds > Vdsat, Vdsat = Vgs − Vt.
β = µCox W/L, Cox = εox/tox.
For pMOS the voltage directions and inequalities reverse.

q: Explain channel length modulation and write the modified saturation current equation.
a: After pinch-off at the point where Vc(y) = VGS − VT0, the effective channel length is L' = L − ΔL, where ΔL (QI = 0) grows with VDS.
Since ID ∝ 1/L', 1/L' ≈ (1/L)(1 + λVDS), λ = CLM coefficient.
ID(SAT) = (µnCox/2)(W/L)(VGS − VT0)²(1 + λVDS).
Creates a discontinuity at VDS = VGS − VT0 unless also applied to ID(lin); λ < 0.1, usually ignored by hand.

q: Explain the substrate bias (body) effect.
a: Equations so far assume VSB = 0 and use VT0.
In two series MOSFETs, VSB of the upper device = VDS of the lower ≠ 0.
VT rises with VSB: VT = VT0 + γ(√(abs(−2φF + VSB)) − √(abs(2φF))), γ = √(2qNAεSi)/Cox.
ID becomes f(VGS, VDS, VSB), non-linear and harder for hand calculation.

q: Derive the expression for threshold voltage including the body effect.
a: Component 1: φGC – work-function difference gate/channel to flatten bands.
Component 2: −2φF – to invert the surface.
Component 3: −QB/Cox – to offset depletion charge QB = −√(2qNAεSi abs(−2φF + VSB)).
Component 4: −Qox/Cox – to offset fixed positive oxide-interface charge.
VT = φGC − 2φF − QB/Cox − Qox/Cox; VT0 uses QB0 (VSB = 0).
VT = VT0 − (QB − QB0)/Cox = VT0 + γ(√(abs(−2φF + VSB)) − √(abs(2φF))).
Signs: nMOS φF −, QB −, γ +, VSB +; pMOS opposite.

q: Explain accumulation, depletion and inversion in the two-terminal MOS structure and give the depletion depth expressions.
a: VG < 0: accumulation – holes gather at the interface.
VG > 0 small: depletion – holes repelled, fixed acceptor ions left; xd = √(2εSi abs(φS − φF)/(qNA)).
VG larger: inversion when surface electron density equals bulk hole density, φS = −φF.
Maximum depletion depth xdm = √(2εSi abs(2φF)/(qNA)); charge Q0 = −qNAxdm = −√(2qNAεSi abs(2φF)).

q: Explain pass-transistor logic and its design requirement.
a: Logic implemented with series/parallel switches (single NMOS or CMOS transmission gate) controlled by inputs; e.g. series A and C → Y = AC.
Requirement: every node must always have a low-resistance path to VDD or ground.
If S1 (controlled by B) opens, Y floats (high impedance); if Y was high, leakage discharges it – not static.
Fix: add S2 controlled by B' from Y to ground, giving a path when B is low.

q: Compare depletion-mode and enhancement-mode nMOS pull-ups.
a: Depletion pull-up: gate tied to source, Vgs = 0, always on; output reaches VDD; transfer curve set by Zpu/Zpd; high dissipation when Vin = 1; non-saturated pull-up gives lower charging resistance.
Enhancement pull-up: high dissipation when Vin = 1; Vout cannot reach VDD (Vt drop); Vgg from a clock phase can cut dissipation; Vgg > VDD needs an extra rail.

q: Derive the pull-up to pull-down ratio for an nMOS inverter driven by another nMOS inverter.
a: Require Vin = Vout = Vinv; take Vinv = 0.5VDD; both devices saturated: Ids = K(W/L)(Vgs − Vt)²/2.
Pull-up (depletion, Vgs = 0): Ids = K(Wpu/Lpu)(−Vtd)²/2.
Pull-down (Vgs = Vinv): Ids = K(Wpd/Lpd)(Vinv − Vt)²/2.
Equal currents: (Wpd/Lpd)(Vinv − Vt)² = (Wpu/Lpu)(−Vtd)²; with Z = L/W: Vinv = Vt − Vtd/√(Zpu/Zpd).
Vt = 0.2VDD, Vtd = −0.6VDD, Vinv = 0.5VDD → √(Zpu/Zpd) = 2 → Zpu/Zpd = 4:1.
Driven via pass transistors the input level is degraded, so Zpu/Zpd ≥ 8:1.

q: Explain the five regions of the CMOS inverter transfer characteristic.
a: Region 1 (A): Vin logic 0 – pMOS on (linear), nMOS off – Vout = VDD, no current.
Region 2 (B): Vin > Vtn – nMOS saturated, pMOS resistive; small current.
Region 3 (C): both saturated – large instantaneous current; VTC very steep.
Region 4 (D): nMOS resistive, pMOS saturated.
Region 5 (E): Vin logic 1 – pMOS off, nMOS on – Vout = 0, no current.

√(βn/βp)(Vin − Vtn) = VDD + Vtp − Vin.
Vin = (VDD + Vtp + Vtn√(βn/βp)) / (1 + √(βn/βp)).
If βn = βp and Vtp = −Vtn → Vin = VDD/2.
β ∝ µW/L and µn = 2.5µp, so Wp/Lp = 2.5 Wn/Ln, i.e. Zpu/Zpd = 2.5:1.

q: State the characteristics of the CMOS inverter and explain why it is preferred to resistor-load NMOS or PMOS inverters.
a: CMOS: no current for logic 1 or 0 input; full rail-to-rail output; p-channel slower than n-channel for same size; current only during transitions, even when driving other CMOS gates.
NMOS + R: Vin = 1 gives constant ID = 5/R; PMOS + R: Vin = 0 gives ID = −5/R; power wasted with no computation.
CMOS: NMOS pull-down and PMOS pull-up each switch off when not pulling.

q: Write the KVL/KCL relations for CMOS inverter analysis and explain the graphical method.
a: VGS(n) = VIN; VGS(p) = VIN − VDD; VDS(n) = VOUT; VDS(p) = VOUT − VDD = VDS(n) − VDD; ID(p) = −ID(n).
Write both I–V equations in terms of VDS(n) and ID(n), plot NMOS curve and PMOS curve (in NMOS variables); their intersection is the operating point.
As VIN rises (0.9 → 4.1 V) VGS(n) increases and VGS(p) becomes less negative, moving the intersection and giving VOUT vs VIN.

q: Explain the effect of process variation and beta ratio on the CMOS VTC.
a: Process corners (good/bad PMOS and NMOS) mostly shift the switching threshold from nominal: strong PMOS/weak NMOS moves it right, weak PMOS/strong NMOS moves it left.
Beta ratio βp/βn ≠ 1 moves switching point from VDD/2: ratios 2, 10 move it higher; 0.5, 0.1 move it lower.

q: Define transconductance gm, output conductance gds and figure of merit ω0.
a: gm = ∂Ids/∂Vgs at constant Vds = β(Vgs − Vt) in saturation – how strongly gate voltage controls current.

q: State the four rules of stick diagrams.
a: Rule 1: sticks of the same type crossing or touching = electrical contact.
Rule 2: sticks of different types crossing or touching = no contact; show contact explicitly if needed.
Rule 3: poly crossing diffusion = transistor; if a contact is shown, it is not a transistor.
Rule 4: in CMOS a demarcation line keeps p-diff away from n-diff; all PMOS on one side, all NMOS on the other.

q: Why are design rules needed? What compromise do they represent?
a: Interface between circuit designer and process engineer; translate stick/symbolic circuits into actual silicon geometry.
Define minimum widths (avoid breaks), spacings (avoid shorts) and overlaps; set by mask resolution and tolerances.
Designer wants tighter, smaller layouts (performance, area); fabricator wants controllable, reproducible processes; compromise gives a competitive circuit at reasonable cost.

q: Compare micron-based and lambda-based design rules.
a: Micron rules: all minimum sizes and spacings in microns; need not be multiples of λ; ~50% area reduction; industry standard.

Lambda rules: scalable CMOS rules based on single parameter λ = half minimum channel length; simple, widely accepted, feature-size independent; minimum feature 2λ; preserve topology; prevent shorts, opens and slipping contacts; MOSIS SCMOS SUBMICRON/DEEPSUBMICRON.

q: State the lambda-based design rules for widths, spacings and contacts with reasons.
a: Widths: poly 2λ, diffusion 2λ, metal 3λ (uneven surface), metal 2 4λ.
Spacings: poly-poly 2λ, metal-metal 2λ (3λ in summary), diff-diff 3λ (depletion spreads), diff-poly λ (avoid unwanted capacitor), metal edge to unconnected layer λ recommended.
Contacts: cut 2λ × 2λ; conductors overlap by λ (misalignment); cut to gate 2λ; cut to cut 2λ (holes merging).
Wells surround transistors by 6λ (12λ between flavours); wiring track 8λ pitch.

q: Explain butting contact and buried contact.
a: Butting contact: connects gate and source of a depletion device – metal contacts both the source diffusion and the poly gate; advantage: no buried contact mask or associated processing.
Buried contact: poly connects directly to diffusion under a buried-contact mask; gate length depends on the mask alignment relative to poly and can vary by λ.
